extracted.intended_audience: readers, students, and practitioners of poetry/literary criticism (those evaluating or aspiring to write heroic/poetic works)
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and apply the essay's criteria for what makes a Poet or heroic poetic work great (qualities of voice, form, moral depth, structure, and enduring effect).

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry as "musical Thought"
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry is 'musical Thought' — at the soul of poetic utterance is perfect music; the Poet is he who thinks in that manner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See deep enough, and you see musically; the heart of Nature being everywhere music. The sound, rhythm, and inner melody of language are essential: where the thought is truly musical, the tones become musical by the greatness, depth and music of the thoughts. Coleridge's remark: musical wording indicates depth and goodness of meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sincerity and depth of vision
rubrics_metrics.description: It is a man's sincerity and depth of vision that makes him a Poet; 'sincerity... we find to be the measure of worth.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: True inward feeling and honest conviction (not mere show or fashionable manner) are the core measure of poetic value; shallow or affected expression cannot establish true poetic status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intensity (world-deep rather than world-wide)
rubrics_metrics.description: Intensity is the prevailing character of genius: 'Dante's greatness has... concentred itself into fiery emphasis and depth' — world-great by being world-deep.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer depth and concentrated force of soul over wide but superficial catholicity; piercing to the heart of Being is more valuable than wide but shallow treatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity beyond the 'show' of greatness
rubrics_metrics.description: Greatness must be real and not merely the 'show' of greatness; people may worship the show, but true admiration is for reality beneath it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Caveat: social trappings can mislead, but sympathetic readers often discern the real dignity ('in the secret heart... it still dimly reveals itself') — evaluate whether the subject/work has intrinsic dignity beyond public image.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thought and work born of suffering / patient labour
rubrics_metrics.description: True thought and great works are often 'the daughter of Pain' — genuine poetic labor is won with toil and suffering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author stresses that Dante's Comedy was written with 'his heart's blood' and 'made me lean for many years': look for evidence that the work arises from deep personal struggle and painstaking craftsmanship rather than superficial facility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genuine Song vs. Prose-in-verse (necessity of rhyme/melody)
rubrics_metrics.description: A right Poem is a Song; if the thought can be spoken plainly it should not be sung; rhyme without inward necessity is 'wooden noise.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: rhyme and jingle with no inward necessity. Advice: only put thought into verse when the inner feeling demands musical utterance; otherwise speak plainly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Architectural harmony / inward symmetry of structure
rubrics_metrics.description: A true inward symmetry, an architectural harmony, should reign in the work: parts proportionate and fitting together (example: Inferno, Purgatorio, Paradiso as compartments of a great edifice).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the work for coherent structural design where sections answer to one another and the whole is proportioned like well-hewn marble stones; the unity of parts supports endurance and truth of the whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power of vision: vivid, decisive painting and condensation
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet must have a great power of vision: 'seizes the very type of a thing; presents that and nothing more' — brevity, abrupt precision, one smiting word.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for concentrated, acute imagery and decisive turns of phrase (examples: Dante's vivid tableaux such as Hall of Dite, 'fiery snow', 'face baked'). Excess verbosity is a weakness; economy that captures the essential likeness is a mark of genius.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sympathy and sincere insight enabling true likeness
rubrics_metrics.description: The ability to 'sympathize' with objects and to be sincere about them is necessary to give real likeness; a man without worth cannot give you the likeness of any object.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the writer shows genuine empathetic engagement with subjects (people, scenes, ideas) rather than vague outwardness or hearsay; sympathetic insight produces authentic portraiture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral earnestness and rigor balanced with pity
rubrics_metrics.description: Moral greatness: 'For rigor, earnestness and depth, he is not to be paralleled' and 'a man who does not know rigor cannot pity either.' Genuine pity must be coupled with moral rigor to avoid sentimental cowardice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check for ethical seriousness and an exacting moral sense that structures compassion; avoid works where pity is merely sentimental or lacks firmness of principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interdependence of parts (each compartment indispensable)
rubrics_metrics.description: Different parts of a great work must support one another (e.g., Inferno without Paradiso would be untrue): 'The Three compartments mutually support one another, are indispensable to one another.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge whether sections are mutually reinforcing; an isolated brilliant part may fail if unintegrated into a coherent whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coherence between worldview/Belief and artistic embodiment
rubrics_metrics.description: The work should be an emblem or embodiment of the author's belief about the universe: Dante's Hell/Purgatory/Paradise are a symbol of his Christian Belief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the artistic representation faithfully expresses an underlying philosophical or moral conception rather than being an arbitrary or purely decorative arrangement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universality and enduring truth (survival beyond fashions)
rubrics_metrics.description: A work that speaks from the inmost parts of a man's soul will endure: 'the inmost is the same yesterday, to-day and forever' — such works address 'true souls' across generations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether the work addresses deep human conditions and truths likely to resonate across ages rather than transient modes of taste or utility metrics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate scope/mode of address (audience and lasting effect)
rubrics_metrics.description: Different great men speak to different audiences and with different effects (e.g., Mahomet to masses with immediate influence; Dante to the noble/pure for long-enduring inspiration).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating impact, distinguish between immediate mass-effect and long-term elevation of the select; lack of worldly empire does not mean lesser greatness — judge suitability of style/mode to intended audience and intended kind of influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elaborated craftsmanship and meticulous finish
rubrics_metrics.description: Great works are elaborated and intensely worked out: 'no work known to me is so elaborated as this of Dante's' — every compartment is 'worked out, with intense earnestness, into truth, into clear visuality.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the care, refinement, and polished workmanship of the text: detailed refinement of each part, not mere raw inspiration, is necessary for great enduring work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to embody an age's soul (spokesman of a people/time)
rubrics_metrics.description: A great poet may serve as the spokesman of an age (Dante as spokesman of the Middle Ages; Shakespeare embodying the Outer Life of Europe).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the work captures and records the characteristic faiths, practices, and sensibilities of its era in a way that makes that era legible to later readers.
